title: Groq's LPU — Determinism Through Static Scheduling
summary: How Groq's LPU achieves determinism. No DRAM: weights live in SRAM (about 10x faster than HBM), so a 70B model spans 576 chips at $15,000-20,000 each. The compiler schedules every instruction, memory access and chip message to the clock cycle — software-defined hardware with no runtime polling; a 2022 paper predicted model latency within 1%. Costs: recompilation on shape change, MoE handled by scatters and gathers, and complexity shifting into the compiler, which Groq now programs with AI. Essentially Kung's systolic array one level up.

chunks.content:
## No DRAM at all

The Groq philosophy takes the opposite extreme: no DRAM at all — the weights live on the chip itself in SRAM, which can be read roughly 10 times faster than even the best HBM. In early 2024 Groq was able to run a Llama 2 70B model at 240 tokens per second, twice as fast as the runner-up. But there is always a catch: the Groq chip (LPU) had only 230 megabytes of SRAM, so a 70 billion parameter model had to be split across 576 chips. At this point the trade is clear: waiting on memory has been exchanged for the overhead of coordinating hundreds of chips, at somewhere between $15,000 and $20,000 per chip.

## Software-defined hardware

Once every operation on the chip has a known duration, everything can be planned ahead. Groq's compiler plans every instruction, every memory access, and every message between chips down to the clock cycle. Google's TPU compiles ahead of time too: its XLA compiler, short for Accelerated Linear Algebra, takes a model's computational graph and emits the instruction stream to run on the chip, splitting the work across multiple TPUs when needed. But XLA only determines the order of instructions, not the exact timing — it cannot, because reads from DRAM take an unpredictable number of clock cycles, so the compiled program starts copying weights from DRAM into the chip and then waits on a flag that flips when the copy is done. Groq's compiler never has to insert that wait. Groq calls it software-defined hardware, because the chip does not get any of the usual responsibilities at runtime: no polling, no checking whether a neighbor's output is ready (clocks still drift and need to be periodically re-synchronized). Determinism has a really convenient consequence: in a 2022 paper Groq engineers predicted the latency of a model before running it and were off by only 1%. In production the same request takes exactly the same number of cycles every time, which brings reliability.

## The costs of determinism

Planning everything ahead does have its own cost. The generated code is very specific to the SRAM and shape of the model being run, so committing more parameters or fewer parameters will trigger a recompilation — that was built intentionally into the compiler, to make sure the processing units are utilized to their full potential. Developers writing CPU code in JAX do something similar called bucketing: they write all the code into buckets of fixed size, and those buckets fit on the processing units. Mixture-of-experts models make queries uneven: at inference time a potentially different set of experts gets activated for every query. The question is what is being statically scheduled — as one engineer put it, a fixed 15-minute slot on the calendar whose meeting can change. The LPU has scatters and gathers: whichever expert is needed is fetched instead, and it still runs for the same amount of time; if experts differ in size, the request can even route to another chip or have that chip change, leaving a little bubble in the pipeline. Determinism gives a lot more ability to predict timing without restricting what you can do. And even with perfect scheduling there is still logical sequencing among chips: each one holds the slice of a model layer, and since the output of layer n is the input of layer n+1, some chips can only execute after others. Groq eases this by streaming intermediate results between layers as soon as they are available — for two consecutive matrix multiplications, row i of z depends only on row i of y.

## Complexity moves into the compiler

The effect of software-defined hardware is that a lot of the complexity moves into the compiler, which becomes harder to write. When Groq was started there were no LLMs to write the software — a small team had to do it all themselves, building a chip that did not have a lot of complexity around the compiler. Today Groq has been using AI to program its LPUs and is getting very good results, because it is easy to wrap your LLM around the problem. Zooming out, Groq ends up echoing Kung's beating heart just at a higher level: the processing elements are the chips themselves, each holding a slice of a layer; the weights are stationary in SRAM, and the activations flow from chip to chip on a schedule fully predetermined by the compiler. Officially Groq's architecture is categorized as dataflow, not systolic, but multiple people have made the connection. Meanwhile the industry keeps producing challengers: an explosion of AI accelerators has raised a lot of venture capital money, facing the "baby turtle problem" — it is going to be very easy to design a chip, but very hard to take one to production.
